newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaraguan leader asks exiles to repatriate assets.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguan leader asks exiles to repatriate assets.

text.p: President-elect Arnoldo Aleman on Monday invited hundreds of thousands of Nicaraguans living abroad to return to their country and said they would be allowed to bring back their money and belongings tax-free.

The invitation was aimed at wealthy Nicaraguans who left during the left-wing Sandinista government of the 1980s and whose money and enterprise are badly needed in one of Latin America's poorest nations.
Thousands of other Nicaraguans also fled during the 43-year dictatorship of the Somoza family. An estimated 200,000 Nicaraguans live in Miami alone.

"To those Nicaraguans who want to return to their country, we say that not only are we going to let them do it free from taxes and free from duties on their vehicles, but they can bring their work equipment free as well," Aleman said,

"This means that those who have a small business or factory in Miami and want to move it to Nicaragua are going to be able to do it tax-free and run it here as they did over there," he said on a television talk show.

Aleman, a former lawyer who leads the right-wing Liberal Alliance coalition, defeated Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega at the polls in October. He will take office on January 10, succeeding outgoing President Violeta Chamorro.

Aleman cautioned that the return of exiles must be gradual so as not to tax Nicaragua's limited infrastructure and called on the U.S. government not to begin a feared mass deportation of Nicaraguans living illegally in the United States.
He said Nicaragua needed time to rebuild its economy and laws to lower the risks for exiles who repatriate assets.
Unemployment in Nicaragua is as high as 50 percent of the work force.
"For this reason we must be pragmatic and a try to minimise the number of Nicaraguans who look for new horizons in their country, and have them return in a slow, non-precipitious fashion," he said.
One lingering political worry centres around land and houses confiscated by the Sandinista government after their 1979 revolution toppled the Somoza regime.

Aleman's promise to reform property laws and compensate former landowners has put him on a potential collision course with the still-powerful Sandinistas, many of whom benefited from the land redistribution.
